name: National Insurance number
issuer: HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC), and on application the Department for Work and Pensions
note: GOV.UK's guides and HMRC's National Insurance Manual NIM39110, read 2026-10-30: two letters, six numbers and a final letter A to D, the same for life; the prefix's letters exclude D, F, I, Q, U and V, the second excludes O, and BG, GB, KN, NK, NT, TN and ZZ aren't used (the pattern holds these; administrative and temporary numbers aren't drawn). A UK resident whose parent claimed Child Benefit is sent it in the 3 months before 16, read as given on registration (the Child Benefit record) from 16, a few months late for the game's simplicity; anyone else living in the UK with the right to work applies, in the UK, and it can take up to 4 weeks. Its holders are asked for it by HMRC and their employer (needed: work, tax); one may start work before it arrives with proof of the right to work. No fee is stated.

sources.title: GOV.UK, National Insurance: Your National Insurance number
sources.said: Your National Insurance number remains the same for life. It’s made up of 2 letters, 6 numbers and a final letter. ... your employer

sources.said: live in the UK ... have the right to work in the UK ... You’ll normally be sent a National Insurance number in the 3 months before your 16th birthday if both the following are true: ... You can only apply when you’re in the UK. ... It can take up to 4 weeks to get your National Insurance number.

sources.title: HMRC internal manual, NIM39110 What a NINO looks like
sources.said: A NINO is made up of 2 letters, 6 numbers and a final letter, which is always A, B, C, or D. ... The characters D, F, I, Q, U, and V are not used as either the first or second letter of a NINO prefix. ... The letter O is not used as the second letter of a prefix. ... Prefixes BG, GB, KN, NK, NT, TN and ZZ are not to be used
